Schaeffler India Limited | Integrated Annual Report 2025

The Schaeffler Group has been driving forward 
groundbreaking inventions and developments in the 
field of motion technology for 80 years. With innovative 
technologies, products, and services for electric mobility, 
CO₂-efficient drives, chassis solutions and renewable 
energies, we are a reliable partner for making motion more 
efficient, intelligent, and sustainable – over the entire 
life cycle. 
Over the decades, Schaeffler has expanded its technological 
footprint through the integration of INA, LuK, FAG, and 
Vitesco strengthening its expertise across bearings, 
clutch systems, powertrain components, and industrial 
applications. The consolidation of these brands under the 
Schaeffler Group in 2002 marked a significant milestone in 
the Company’s evolution as a diversified motion technology 
enterprise.
Schaeffler operates with around 110,000 employees and 
more than 250 locations in 55 countries, one of the world’s 
largest family-owned companies and one of Germany’s most 
innovative companies.
Vision:  
Becoming the leading Motion 
Technology Company 
Schaeffler never stands still. We embrace challenges 
to develop breakthrough innovations and advance 
technological progress. With our pioneering spirit, we 
relentlessly go forward to support our customers with 
the best solutions.
Mission: 
We offer innovative products and 
services in the field of motion
Our mission expresses how we realise our purpose and our 
vision. For decades, fulfilling our customers’ needs with 
innovative products and services has been the backbone of 
Schaeffler’s success. And it continues to be.

Schaeffler India Limited | Integrated Annual Report 2025

Schaeffler India’s sixth Integrated Report presents a 
comprehensive overview of how the Company creates 
sustainable value through deliberate alignment of strategy, 
governance, performance, risk management, ESG priorities, 
and outlook for the financial year ended December 31, 2025. 
The report seeks to provide stakeholders with a balanced, 
transparent, and forward-looking account of how the 
Company creates and sustains value over the short, medium, 
and long-term.
The Integrated Report reflects Schaeffler India’s commitment 
to disciplined performance, enterprise resilience, and 
responsible business conduct. It brings together financial 
and non-financial information to present a cohesive 
view of value creation across strategic, operational, and 
sustainability dimensions.
As a leading motion technology Company, Schaeffler 
India operates at the intersection of engineering, mobility 
transformation, industrial productivity, and sustainability 
expectations. In this environment, value creation depends 
not only on financial performance but on the effective 
management and enhancement of multiple forms of capital. 
The Company’s integrated approach ensures that strategic 
decisions, capital allocation, and operational priorities are 
evaluated through a long-term value lens. 
Corporate Overview
Value creation across the six capitals
Schaeffler India’s business model transforms inputs across 
six capitals into sustainable outcomes:
•	
Human Capital 
Leadership continuity, technical 
capability, and a culture 
grounded in safety, compliance, 
and accountability underpin 
operational resilience and 
innovation capacity.
•	
Social and Relationship Capital 
Trusted partnerships with customers, 
suppliers, regulators, and 
communities reinforce reliability, 
responsible conduct, and 
ecosystem strength.
•	
Natural Capital 
Resource efficiency initiatives, 
energy optimisation, emissions 
management, and responsible 
sourcing practices reflect the 
Company’s commitment to 
environmental stewardship.
The integration of these capitals is central to Schaeffler 
India’s strategy. Growth initiatives are aligned with 
financial prudence. Manufacturing investments incorporate 
sustainability considerations. Innovation priorities address 
evolving mobility and industrial needs. Governance oversight 
ensures accountability and risk discipline across 
the enterprise.
By presenting financial and non-financial performance 
together, this report provides stakeholders with a connected 
view of how Schaeffler India sustains enterprise resilience 
while delivering disciplined performance.
Scope and boundary of the report
This Integrated Report covers the financial year from 
January 01, 2025 to December 31, 2025.
The report pertains to Schaeffler India Limited and includes 
disclosures related to its manufacturing plants, research and 
development centres, and corporate offices located in India. 
Financial information is based on the audited standalone 
financial statements of Schaeffler India Limited.
Non-financial and sustainability disclosures relate to the 
Company’s Indian operations, unless otherwise specified. 
Where relevant, references to the Schaeffler Group are 
included for strategic context; however, operational and 
performance data presented herein relate specifically to 
Schaeffler India Limited.

Our Distinctive Edge
Our distinctive strength lies in seamlessly integrating deep engineering expertise, a broad portfolio, and disciplined execution 
into a unified value creation model. Supported by the Schaeffler Group’s global heritage and fortified by a strong manufacturing 
and customer presence in India, we blend comprehensive system insight with operational excellence to consistently deliver 
sustained performance and tangible value for our customers.
Our value proposition is defined across six inter-linked dimensions:
(Intellectual Capital | Material themes: 
Innovation, technology leadership)
We leverage the Group’s comprehensive expertise 
across all aspects of motion with delivering 
integrated solutions that optimise performance 
across vehicle and industrial systems. By 
combining mechanical engineering with 
electronics and digital technologies, we support 
the advancement of mobility platforms, electrified 
drive trains, and smart industrial systems.
(Financial Capital | Material themes: Revenue 
resilience, portfolio diversification)
A diversified portfolio across Automotive 
Technologies, Vehicle Lifetime Solutions, and 
Bearings & Industrial Solutions creates structural 
balance, enhancing resilience through demand 
cycles. This supports performance, cash flow, 
disciplined capital allocation, and sustained 
performance amid market volatility.
(Manufactured Capital | Material themes: Quality, 
productivity, supply chain reliability)
Our state-of-the-art manufacturing facilities in 
India, supported by robust quality systems and 
process excellence, ensure reliable delivery. 
Precision production, continuous productivity 
gains, and strict cost discipline enhance 
competitiveness while upholding high performance 
standards. Operational discipline is central to 
our execution.
(Human Capital | Material themes: Capability 
building, leadership continuity, safety)
Our performance is driven by engineering 
expertise, stable leadership, and a culture 
of accountability and compliance. Ongoing 
capability development fuels innovation and 
operational resilience, while technical depth and 
disciplined governance empower us to navigate 
transformation effectively.
(Social and Relationship Capital | Material 
themes: Customer trust, responsible business 
conduct)
Long-standing partnerships with OEMs, 
industrial clients, suppliers, and service 
providers reinforce value chain reliability. Our 
customer-centric approach extends beyond 
supply to include engineering support, training, 
and lifecycle solutions, building strong 
stakeholder trust through dependable delivery 
and quality.
(Natural Capital | Material themes: Energy 
efficiency, emissions management, sustainable 
operations)
Energy efficiency, resource optimisation, and 
environmental management are integral to our 
operations. Sustainability drives product design, 
manufacturing, and supply chain decisions, 
underscoring our commitment to responsible, 
long-term industrial growth.

It gives me immense pleasure to share that Schaeffler 
India delivered another year of exemplary performance, 
demonstrating the strength of a business built on operational 
excellence, financial prudence, and institutional stability.
The year unfolded in an environment characterised by evolving 
mobility ecosystems, shifting industrial cycles, and continued 
global economic uncertainty. Demand patterns across sectors 
remained dynamic, supply chains continued to recalibrate 
and cost environments required careful navigation. Yet 
amid this variability, Schaeffler India sustained its growth 
trajectory while strengthening the quality and resilience of 
its earnings. The outcome reflects the Company’s structural 
strengths – a balanced portfolio across automotive and 
industrial businesses, disciplined capital allocation, and 
mature operating systems that enable consistency across 
cycles. Strong cash generation, stable margins, and reliable 
delivery performance reaffirm Schaeffler India’s ability to 
convert strategic intent into measurable outcomes allowing the 
Company to align with India’s growth trajectory.
India is in a new industrial era, propelled by scale, resilience, 
and ambition. Ranked among the fastest-growing economies 
globally, it is on track to become the world’s third-largest 
economy. While there are recent adjustments to the country’s 
growth outlook to neutral due to emerging domestic and 
global challenges, India is still expected to maintain its status 
as one of the fastest-growing major economies, albeit at a 
more moderated pace compared to previous high-growth 
periods. Over the year, this performance was supported by 
multiple factors such as robust domestic demand, Income Tax 
and Goods and Services Tax rationalisation, softer crude oil 
prices and front-loading of government capital expenditure. 
Schaeffler India is committed to be a part of this growth story 
by driving innovation in mobility solutions, strengthening 
localisation, expanding manufacturing footprint, and investing 
in sustainable technologies that support the nation’s long-term 
economic momentum.
Eranti Sumithasri 
Chairwoman
Dear 
Stakeholders,
Leading with Strength
Schaeffler India sustained its growth 
trajectory while strengthening the quality 
and resilience of its earnings. The outcome 
reflects the Company’s structural strengths – 
a balanced portfolio across automotive and 
industrial businesses, disciplined capital 
allocation, and mature operating systems 
that enable consistency across cycles.
The automotive industry is undergoing a transformative shift 
driven by rising consumer demand for sustainable mobility and 
regulatory requirements to reduce carbon emissions. However, 
the evolving geopolitical environment and potential disruptions 
in crude supply present significant challenges to India’s growth 
trajectory and the automotive sector’s progress. Schaeffler 
India remains confident that its robust product portfolio and 
technological capabilities equip to navigate these uncertainties 
and continue driving sector development. The organisation 
has always been committed to sustainability and will continue 
to build on this foundation as the industry evolves. The new 
manufacturing facility at Shoolagiri, Tamil Nadu, reflects 
commitment to strengthening stakeholder value. With the set 
up of the E-Axle production line at Talegaon, Schaeffler India 
has strengthened its capabilities in electric mobility, supporting 
India’s transition towards cleaner and sustainable motion. 
India’s industrial sector is strongly driven by manufacturing 
expansion in electronics, automobiles, and basic metals, 
supported by government schemes and robust export 
momentum. Increasing Index of Industrial Production figures 
and core industry output reflect this positive trajectory, 
despites global trade uncertainties. Through portfolio 
expansion, advance manufacturing capabilities, innovation, 
and strategic localisation, Schaeffler India continues to  
support this growth.

Resilience as a structural advantage
One of the defining characteristics of Schaeffler India is its 
enterprise resilience, the capacity to maintain stability and 
performance despite external volatility.
A diversified presence across automotive and industrial 
businesses provides balance through economic cycles. 
Operational maturity in manufacturing, supply chain, and 
quality systems enables the Company to respond with agility to 
changing conditions. Even as external environments fluctuate, 
Schaeffler India has consistently upheld its commitments 
to customers in reliability, product quality, and delivery 
performance. 
This is further reinforced by the Company’s deep localisation 
strategy, robust supplier ecosystem, and strong engineering 
capabilities, which together enhance resilience while 
supporting long-term competitiveness. 
Importantly, resilience at Schaeffler India is about designing 
the enterprise in a way that enables stability, adaptability, and 
sustainable performance over time.
Financial discipline and capital 
stewardship
Sustained value creation requires a careful balance between 
growth ambition and financial discipline.
During the year, Schaeffler India continued to demonstrate 
strong capital stewardship, supported by healthy operating 
cash flows and prudent approach to investment. Capital 
allocation decisions remain guided by long-term strategic 
priorities while maintaining balance sheet strength and 
financial flexibility.
The Company continues to invest in technology capabilities, 
advanced manufacturing, digitisation, and innovation 
initiatives that strengthen its competitive positioning across 
evolving mobility and industrial landscapes. At the same time, 
disciplined cost management and operational efficiency remain 
integral to maintaining profitability and resilience.
Creating value beyond business
Schaeffler India’s work in water conservation, access to 
education, and climate resilience are designed to create 
measurable impact and long term stability. Initiatives on 
water conservation, HOPE Engineering Scholarships and 
agro forestry exemplify this commitment. By integrating 
technological advancement with human progress, the Company 
ensures that its growth is inseparable from the well being of 
the communities we serve. I am pleased to share that this 
year too, Schaeffler India has been honoured with awards 
for water preservation initiatives and for its work in women 
empowerment and inclusion. These are a few among the many 
recognitions we have received for CSR efforts.
Institutional strength and governance
Institutional capability remains Schaeffler India’s most 
enduring strengths. 
The Company benefits from a leadership team with deep 
domain expertise, supported by a workforce committed to 
excellence and accountability. Together, they uphold the 
Company’s high standards of quality, safety, integrity, and 
compliance driving sustainable growth and long-term 
value creation. 
Strong governance frameworks further reinforce this 
foundation. Transparent processes, disciplined risk 
management, and effective leadership oversight ensure that 
the organisation remains responsive to emerging opportunities 
and challenges while maintaining strategic discipline. 
During the year, the Board also witnessed certain transitions. 
Mr. Dharmesh Arora and Mr. Amit Kalyani stepped down from 
the Board to pursue other professional commitments. On

Automotive Technologies and Vehicle Lifetime Solutions 
drive growth through platform wins and localisation while 
the Bearings & Industrial Solutions division offers counter-
cyclical stability, particularly in railways and industrial 
applications. Together, these businesses reduce reliance on 
any single end-market and smoothen earnings volatility.

to perform. Sustainable performance emerges when 
growth initiatives are aligned with financial prudence and 
operational discipline. Revenue and margin progression 
and healthy cash flows moving in tandem demonstrate that

on strong controls and robust risk management.  During the 
year, we enhanced frameworks around cybersecurity, counter 
party exposure, and treasury risk, while actively managing 
interest rate and currency volatility.

remains balanced – funding growth, maintaining balance 
sheet strength, and returning cash to Shareholders. Dividend 
decisions are guided by sustainable earnings and cash flow 
visibility, alongside ROCE and free cash flow conversion.

Engineering during  
regulatory transition
The shift to the new emission norms in the tractor segment 
changed how engines behaved, leading to higher risks of 
torsional vibration and rattle noise. We addressed these 
challenges through system-level modelling and driveline 
optimisation.
•	
Redesigned systems for a leading tractor platform 
helping reduce fluctuations by about 60%. This 
eliminated rattling noises at the vehicle level, making 
the overall performance more stable and reliable. 
•	
Refined the system to reduce friction effects using 
simulation‑led development for high-power tractor 
segment for a leading OEM. 
•	
Our analysis revealed that lower flywheel inertia was 
causing unwanted vibrations. By fine-tuning the engine 
speed, increasing the flywheel weight, and boosting 
the drivetrain’s inertia, we successfully reduced these 
vibrations to below the engine’s natural levels—resulting 
in smoother and more reliable performance.
These collaborations highlight the growing role of 
increasing system-level engineering and simulation in 
driveline optimisation, reinforcing our position as a trusted  
technology partner.
Validation as risk mitigation
Robust validation is key to ensuring performance credibility. 
During 2025, Schaeffler India successfully conducted 
gradient launch validation for a major project, completing 
143 launches on an 18% incline—surpassing the required 
100—with zero clutch slippage. This achievement marks the 
first time this rigorous validation method has been executed 
in India by our Vehicle Engineering team, underscoring our 
unwavering commitment to lifecycle reliability and building 
lasting customer trust.
The growing conversion of disclosures into formal filings 
underscores the maturity of our IP governance processes. 
Engineering outcomes are increasingly assessed not only 
for performance and customer relevance, but also 
for defensibility.

Engineering material efficiency 
at scale
Material efficiency lies at the core of our manufacturing 
discipline. In precision engineering, waste not only poses 
an environmental challenge but also signals economic 
inefficiency. We are continuously advancing our circular 
economy initiatives by actively reducing waste generation, 
enhancing material recovery processes, and minimising 
reliance on landfill disposal.
Plastic waste management and 
Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR)
Schaeffler India Limited operates under the Plastic Waste 
Management (PWM) Rules, 2016, as a brand owner and 
importer of plastic-packaged automotive products in the 
Indian market. In 2025, we successfully met our Extended 
Producer Responsibility (EPR) obligations through well-
structured compliance frameworks and strategic partnerships 
with authorised recyclers.
We generated approximately 591 metric tonnes of End-of-
Life (EoL) credits and recycled 295 metric tonnes of plastic 
waste, securing the necessary recycling credits in full 
accordance with regulatory mandates. Our adherence to the 
PWM framework is ensured through rigorous documentation, 
prompt reporting, and ongoing monitoring of 
statutory requirements.
By executing these responsibilities with discipline and 
actively engaging in the formal recycling ecosystem, we 
demonstrate our unwavering commitment to responsible 
plastic waste management, regulatory compliance, and 
environmentally sustainable operations. Our strong recovery 
performance is a testament to enhanced waste segregation 
systems, authorised recycling collaborations, and meticulous 
material tracking processes.
Zero waste to landfill: A journey of 
operational discipline
A significant environmental milestone for Schaeffler 
India was the attainment of Zero Waste to Landfill 
across all manufacturing sites. This accomplishment 
underscores our sustained commitment to enhancing 
waste segregation, strengthening recycling 
partnerships, and implementing rigorous traceability 
systems for manufacturing waste streams.
Although some landfill use occurred at select sites early 
in the year, operational improvements throughout the 
reporting period enabled all facilities to achieve and 
sustain Zero Waste to Landfill status.
We remain vigilant in monitoring non-recycled waste 
ratios and are dedicated to continuously improving 
waste recovery practices to ensure ongoing elimination 
of landfill dependency across our operations.
Water stewardship and circular 
resource management
Responsible water management is a cornerstone of Schaeffler 
India’s environmental performance. Through targeted process 
optimisation and proactive water conservation initiatives, 
we conserved 15,935 cubic metres of freshwater during the 
reporting year.
Furthermore, we have implemented rainwater harvesting 
systems across multiple sites, enhancing groundwater 
recharge and bolstering long-term water resilience.
We remain committed to continuously exploring 
opportunities to improve water efficiency and progress 
steadily toward our long-term goal of achieving 
water neutrality.
Schaeffler India has articulated a water 
neutrality ambition by 2030.
Environmental management and governance
At Schaeffler India, our commitment to environmental performance is underpinned by robust governance frameworks and 
stringent operational controls. All manufacturing facilities operate within certified environmental management systems, 
rigorously aligned with internationally recognised standards.
We proactively monitor key environmental indicators—including emissions, energy consumption, waste generation, and water 
usage—across all operational sites. Beyond tracking greenhouse gases, we vigilantly measure air pollutants such as nitrogen 
oxides (NOx), sulphur oxides (SOx), volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and particulate matter, ensuring full compliance with 
environmental regulations while championing responsible stewardship.

Conserving water, 
reviving livelihoods
The Jal Jeevika project, implemented by BAIF with 
CSR support from Schaeffler India Limited, addressed 
chronic water scarcity in Mal and Samot villages 
despite high rainfall. Using a ridge-to-valley watershed 
approach, 950 hectares were treated between 
2022–2025, directly benefiting 477+ farmers.
The project harvested 15.7 lakh cubic metres of water, 
improved groundwater levels, and expanded irrigated 
land. Farmers shifted from single-season to multi-
season cropping, raising annual household incomes  
up to ₹30,000–₹35,000. 
Local employment worth ₹29 lakhs was generated, 
alongside community contributions and strengthened 
village institutions.
Seasonal migration reduced, food security improved, 
and community confidence grew. Jaljeevika 
demonstrates how scientific watershed planning, 
community participation, and CSR partnerships can 
build water-secure, resilient tribal landscapes.
Cultivating stability 
through agroforestry
Chintaman Bagul, a small farmer from Gopalpura, 
struggled with low productivity and seasonal migration, 
earning only ₹25,000–₹30,000 annually. In 2024, 
through the Wadi Agroforestry Project at surgana taluka 
in Nashik district of Maharashtra (implemented by 
BAIF with CSR support from Schaeffler), he converted 
one acre of barren land into an orchard with 80 mango 
grafts and 200 forestry plants, supported by solar 
irrigation and training.
Within the first season, he harvested 19 quintals of 
turmeric, selling 16 quintals for ₹1,12,000—nearly four 
times his previous income. The intervention ended his 
need for migration, improved household stability, and 
positioned him as a self-reliant farmer with sustainable 
livelihood prospects.

4. Responsibilities of the Board and Committees
Board as a Trustee 
•
The Board consists of distinguished professionals with
diverse skills and experience. It operates with complete
information, good faith, due diligence, and care, always 
prioritising the best interests of the Company and its 
Shareholders. The Board exercises independent and
objective judgement in corporate matters.
As at the end of financial year, the Board comprises 38%
Independent Directors. This underscores the Company’s 
commitment to maintaining Board independence
and ensuring fair treatment of minority 
Shareholders’ interests.
•
As a good governance practice to strengthen the
independence of the Board, the roles of Chief Executive
Officer and Chairperson are separated. The Chairperson
is a woman Independent Director, while the CEO
is an Executive Director. This structure aligns with
discretionary regulatory requirements and promotes 
balanced and effective leadership.
•
Independent Directors hold separate meetings, without 
Executive Directors or Senior Executives, to evaluate the
Board’s overall performance.
•
The Board reviews and provides guidance on corporate
strategy, major plans of action, corporate governance,
compliance framework, risk management policies 
and procedures, annual budgets, and business plans.
The Board sets performance objectives, monitors its 
implementation and corporate performance.
Performance Review  
•
The Board regularly carries out evaluation to appraise its 
performance and assess whether it possesses the right 
mix of backgrounds and competences. Familiarisation
and training programmes for Directors are conducted
periodically, including plant visits, interactions with
the Executive Leadership team, strategy meetings, and
engagements with statutory auditors. These initiatives 
enable Directors, particularly Non-Executive Directors,
to gain a comprehensive understanding of the
Company’s operations.
•
The Nomination and Remuneration Committee, along
with the Board, conducts performance evaluations for
the Board of Directors, its Committees and individual 
Directors. Directors are evaluated based on criteria
such as attendance, preparedness for meetings,
staying informed on relevant developments, active
participation, and constructive contributions during
discussions. Special emphasis is placed on their ability 
to protect the interests of all Shareholders and to engage
with the management team thoughtfully challenging
ideas without being confrontational or obstructive. The
Board annually assesses the independence, integrity,
expertise, and experience of Independent Directors to
ensure these standards are met. Annual confirmations 
of independence are obtained from all Independent 
Directors to reaffirm their status and compliance with
regulatory requirements.
Succession Planning 
•
The Board reviews and approves the adequacy 
of the Company’s policies, plans and procedures 
concerning succession planning in accordance with the
recommendations of the Nomination and
Remuneration Committee.
Board and Committee Composition 
•
5 (Five) Board-level committees have adopted charters 
defining the roles and duties of each Committee to
support the Board in performing its functions.
•
Committee mandate, composition and working
procedures are well defined by the Board based on
the specific skill requirements of each Committee.

Overview
In an environment shaped by macroeconomic variability, 
technology transition, supply chain reconfiguration, climate 
volatility, and regulatory complexity, resilience is engineered. 
In response to these multifaceted challenges, we have 
adopted a comprehensive approach to risk management that 
is embedded in governance, integrated with planning, and 
aligned to capital discipline. It safeguards continuity while 
enabling strategic growth.
The Risk Management System (RMS) of Schaeffler India 
Limited aims to establish an effective and efficient system 
that is fully embedded in the Schaeffler Group’s governance 
framework. The Risk Management System is integrated across 
all divisions, functions and plants of Schaeffler India Limited.
Governance framework
Our fundamental philosophy of corporate governance is 
to achieve business excellence and commit to enhancing 
long-term stakeholder value while considering the needs and 
interests of all its stakeholders. We believe that governance 
practices allow the management to efficiently direct and 
control the affairs of the Company, thereby achieving our goal 
of maximising value for all its stakeholders.
Risk Management is an integral part of our governance 
structure, with prudent and well-defined risk management 
practices and policies enabling businesses to protect the 
interests of all stakeholders. We have adopted a multi-
layered process involving the entire organisation, right from 
the risk operators to the Board of Directors.
Risk management – an important 
constituent of corporate governance
The Risk Management System is embedded in our 
governance structure, aimed at coordinating the activities 
of the governance sub-systems subordinate to the Board of 
Directors, comprising the Compliance Management System, 
Risk Management System, Internal Control System and 
Internal Audit.

coordination with the Internal Control System (ICS), the 
Compliance Management System (CMS) and Internal Audit

Executive Context
Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A)
1. Executive context
FY2025 unfolded in an environment defined more by 
divergence than synchronised recovery. While headline 
macro indicators pointed to stabilisation after years of 
inflation shocks, supply chain disruptions, and policy 
tightening, the quality of growth and the allocation of capital 
remained uneven across geographies and sectors.
For engineering-led industries, this mattered because 
investment decisions were driven by long-duration themes 
rather than near-term cyclicality. Electrification, renewable 
power, industrial automation, and supply chain localisation 
became structural magnets for capital, policy attention, 
and technology roadmaps. Motion technologies sit at the 
intersection of these shifts. They enable efficiency, reliability, 
energy conversion, and system integration across vehicles, 
factories, railways, and renewable assets.
Against this backdrop, India’s macro trajectory remained 
a standout. India portrayed scale and resilience, driven by 
public investment, strong demand, and better manufacturing 
policies. This divergence from global growth patterns 
strengthened India’s relevance not only as an end market, 
but as a production and engineering hub. For Schaeffler 
India Limited, the year was therefore less about navigating 
uncertainty alone and more about translating a structural 
opportunity into disciplined execution– building capacity, 
deepening localisation, protecting service levels, and 
strengthening portfolio balance. The Company’s strategic 
positioning as The Motion Technology Company is reflected 
in how it invests, how it allocates resources across end-
markets, and how it manages risk through portfolio design 
rather than reactive cost action.
2. Macroeconomic environment
2.1 Global economy
According to the World Bank, global growth in 2025 averaged 
2.7%, shaped by offsetting forces like trade policy headwinds 
on one side and the fading impact of monetary easing, fiscal 
support, and technology investments on the other. While the 
post-pandemic recovery was strong, it remained uneven and 
came at the cost of elevated inflation and debt. 
Inflation moderated across most economies, moving closer to 
central bank targets, with interest rates beginning to decline. 
Growth in advanced economies proved resilient despite
rising trade tensions and policy uncertainty. However, the 
outlook ahead is expected to be tempered by the lingering 
effects of tariff hikes and heightened vulnerability to shifts in 
trade and fiscal policies.
The United States benefited from relative demand resilience 
and investment in advanced manufacturing and technology, 
while Europe faced persistent industrial softness amid
energy transition costs and external demand constraints. 
For industrial supply chains, this environment translated 
into more selective capital flows and a higher premium on
reliability, quality execution, and localisation especially for 
components and systems tied to electrification and efficiency 
improvements.
Global economic conditions in 2025 presented a mix of 
downsides and upsides. Trade tensions, tighter financial 
conditions, heightened geopolitical stress, and the risks of 
natural disasters. At the same time, private sector adaptation 
helped reduce the drag from higher trade barriers, while 
technology led investments supported productivity gains. 
Against this backdrop, key global challenges remain – 
diversifying trade partnerships amid rising frictions and 
responding effectively to changing climate patterns and 
extreme weather events.
2.2 Indian economy
The Reserve Bank of India revised its GDP growth forecast for 
FY2025-26 upward to 7.4% from the earlier estimate of 6.8%, 
reflecting robust domestic demand, rationalisation of income 
and goods and services taxes, softer crude oil prices, and
the front loading of government capital expenditure. India 
continues to stand out as one of the world’s fastest growing 
major economies, well positioned to sustain this momentum. 
While global growth remained steady but below historical 
averages, India’s growth profile continued to be supported
by infrastructure spending, services strength, and steady 
manufacturing activity creating a structurally attractive 
environment for engineering-intensive companies.
A defining feature of India’s policy landscape has been the 
deliberate use of public capital expenditure as an economic 
engine. Central government capex has expanded materially 
over the past five years. Union Budget cycle indicate that 
capex levels rose from roughly `4.5 lakh crore in FY2021 to 
~`11.2 lakh crore for FY2025–26 (with revised estimates 
discussed in the FY2026–27 budget context). This creates 
demand visibility for railways, roads, energy, defence and 
manufacturing-linked sectors. Importantly, capex-led growth 
supports downstream ecosystems such as improvement in 
logistics efficiency and increased industrial utilisation. This 
means a broader and more stable set of end-demand drivers 
beyond vehicle production cycles alone.
Policy continuity has also supported manufacturing 
competitiveness through Production Linked Incentive 
(PLI) schemes and localisation incentives. Manufacturing

of 2025, signalling stable production conditions. For 
companies with deep engineering capability, localisation is 
no longer only a cost advantage; it is a resilience advantage. 
It reduces exposure to cross-border logistics volatility, 
shortens response time for customers, and improves the 
ability to scale programs with tighter timelines. Beyond 
domestic growth drivers, India’s external trade architecture 
is also evolving. The conclusion of negotiations for the 
India–EU Free Trade Agreement marks a defining milestone 
in deepening market integration between India and 
European Union. For engineering‑intensive companies, 
this partnership is expected to expand access to advanced 
markets, align standards, and create new opportunities in 
automotive, industrial, and energy value chains. As India 
strengthens its role in global supply networks, Schaeffler 
India’s localisation and capacity investments are positioned 
not only as resilience enablers but to open access to global 
opportunities.
For Schaeffler India, the strategic relevance of the automotive 
cycle lies in the engineering roadmap. As customers pivot 
to hybrid, electrified, and efficiency-optimised platforms, 
the Company’s positioning is strengthened by its ability 
to bring global platform expertise into India and localise 
manufacturing. This is particularly critical as OEMs demand 
tighter localisation, faster program launches, and predictable 
quality performance. The Company’s investments and 
capacity actions during the year are consistent with this 
shift – engineering and industrialisation capability becomes 
a prerequisite to win and execute programs, not merely a 
differentiator in the sales cycle.
3. Industry overview
3.1 Automotive industry 
India’s automotive industry in FY2025 reflected a 
normalisation pattern – certain segments moderated after 
strong growth in the earlier recovery phase, while structural 
drivers continued to reshape platform requirements. 
Passenger vehicles remained supported by a GST 
moderation, SUV-led mix, urban consumption resilience, 
and expanding model portfolios. Two-wheelers showed 
gradual recovery, with rural demand sensitivity influenced by 
income cycles and financing conditions. Commercial vehicles 
moderated in line with freight cycle normalisation.
Electrification added another layer of complexity. While internal 
combustion engine platforms remain dominant in absolute 
volumes, electrification penetration continues to increase 
in specific pockets particularly in two-wheelers and certain 
passenger vehicle categories. In Electric Passenger Vehicles, 
while battery electric vehicles (BEVs) are seeing adoption, hybrid 
electric vehicles (HEVs) and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) have seen 
a resurgence due to their ability to offer immediate emission 
reductions without relying on extensive, yet-to-be-developed 
charging infrastructure. For Schaeffler India, the strategic 
relevance of the automotive cycle lies in the engineering roadmap. 
As customers pivot to hybrid, electrified, and efficiency-optimised 
platforms, the Company’s positioning is strengthened by its 
ability to bring global platform expertise into India and localise 
manufacturing. This is particularly critical as OEMs demand tighter 
localisation, faster program launches, and predictable quality 
performance. The Company’s investments and capacity actions 
during the year are consistent with this shift – engineering and 
industrialisation capability becomes a prerequisite to win and 
execute programs, not merely a differentiator in the sales cycle.

Emerging trends 
The automotive industry is undergoing a transformative 
shift, led by the rapid adoption of electric vehicles. Rising 
consumer demand for sustainable mobility, regulatory 
pressures to reduce carbon emissions, and advancements 
in battery technology are accelerating this transition. New 
opportunities for collaboration are emerging as battery 
manufacturing hubs take shape in regions such as Europe 
and the U.S., reshaping traditional supply chains and 
spurring investments in critical resources like lithium and 
cobalt. At the same time, Industry 4.0 technologies including 
Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, IoT, and robotics are 
redefining manufacturing processes, enhancing productivity, 
reducing costs, and enabling new business models centered 
on smart factories and connected vehicles.
Challenges
Despite these opportunities, India’s automotive sector faces 
structural challenges. Although the country is the fourth 
largest automobile producer globally, its share in the $20 
billion global automotive component trade remains modest 
at around 3%, with particularly low representation in high 
precision segments such as engine components, drive 
transmission, and steering systems. Operational costs, 
infrastructural gaps, moderate integration into global value 
chains, and limited R&D expenditure continue to constrain 
competitiveness. Addressing these challenges will be critical 
for India to strengthen its position in the global automotive 
ecosystem and fully leverage the opportunities presented by 
electrification and digital transformation.
Vision 2030
NITI Aayog has outlined an ambitious yet achievable vision 
for India’s automotive sector by 2030. The roadmap projects 
automotive component production expanding to $145 
billion, with exports tripling from $20 billion to $60 billion. 
This trajectory would generate a trade surplus of nearly $25 
billion and significantly increase India’s share in the global 
automotive value chain from 3% to 8%. Beyond economic 
gains, this growth is expected to create 2.5 million new jobs, 
raising total direct employment in the sector to between 3–4 
million, thereby reinforcing the sector’s role as a driver of 
industrial growth and social progress.

The Indian automotive aftermarket remains structurally 
attractive and comparatively resilient across economic 
cycles. Industry research has estimated long-term growth 
in the mid-to-high single digits, supported by an expanding 
vehicle parc, increasing average vehicle age, rising utilisation 
in multiple segments, and a growing preference for cost-
efficient maintenance. 
Over time, the market is also formalising, with organised 
distribution channels increasing penetration. Consumers 
are showing a greater willingness to adopt branded, quality-
assured components, and digital integration is becoming 
more common in parts procurement and service workflows.
Lifecycle businesses carry strategic importance beyond 
revenue contribution. They provide stability when original 
equipment cycles moderate, they can support stronger and 
more stable margins due to value-added services and brand 
premium, and they deepen customer proximity. A meaningful 
lifecycle share of revenue improves predictability of cash 
flows and reduces concentration risk. 
3.2 Industrial sector
Industrial demand during FY2025 remained supported by 
policy-backed investments and long-term structural trends. 
Automation adoption continued across manufacturing, 
reshaping industrial operations through advanced robotics, 
AI driven analytics, and IoT enabled systems. Industries 
leveraged these technologies to streamline production, 
enhance precision, reduce costs, and improve flexibility. The 
integration of smart automation not only boosted productivity 
but also strengthened resilience against supply chain 
disruptions, while enabling new business models centered on 
connected factories and data-driven decision making.
Export momentum remained strong in 2025, led by 
robust growth in engineering goods, pharmaceuticals, 
and chemicals, which collectively boosted overall export 
performance. Core industries displayed mixed but generally 
positive trends, with coal and refinery products contributing 
meaningfully to industrial output. Together, these factors 
underscored the resilience of India’s industrial base while 
highlighting the importance of sectoral diversification in 
sustaining growth.
3.2.1 Railways
Indian Railways continued its transformation journey in 
becoming a world class network, which was guided by 
innovation and focused efforts. With a strong focus on 
modern infrastructure and enhanced connectivity, Indian 
Railways is fuelling national growth by offering better 
passenger experience and efficient transport solution.
Infrastructure expansion remained robust, with over 900 
kilometers of new track commissioned between April and 
November 2025. Sectional speeds were raised to 130 kmph 
across 599 track kilometers and to 110 kmph across 4,069 
kilometers, supported by advanced track machinery and 
upgrades across the Golden Quadrilateral, Golden Diagonal, 
and other key routes.
Electrification efforts advanced in mission mode, with 99.2% 
of the Broad-Gauge network now electrified well ahead of 
global peers such as the UK (39%), Russia (52%), and China 
(82%). 14 Railway Zones and 25 States/Union Territories
have achieved 100% electrification, underscoring India’s 
leadership in sustainable rail operations. Complementing 
these achievements, increasing capacity of locos & coaches, 
quadruple tracking across high density lines, station 
redevelopment, enhanced safety systems, wider adoption of 
digital technologies, and expansion of freight corridors have 
reinforced Indian Railways as a key driver of national growth. 
Collectively, these initiatives are laying the foundation for
a future-ready rail network that is faster, safer, greener, and 
more inclusive.
3.2.3 Two-wheelers
India’s two-wheeler sector witnessed a broad-based recovery 
in 2025, with total registrations crossing 2.02 crore units, 
about 7% higher than in 2024. This marks a sustained up-
cycle and brings the sector close to pre-pandemic volumes. 
The GST 2.0 restructuring significantly improved affordability 
and has been a key driver of economic growth.

Electric two-wheelers emerged as structural driver, with 
volumes crossing 1.2 million units in 2025, registering 
~21% year-on-year growth and accounting for nearly 58% of 
India’s total EV market. The industry now operates on a dual 
track model – ICE are generating profits which are used as 
an investment in EVs whereas EV focused OEMs are using 
software to drive revenue. 
Seasonal factors also played a role, with November 2025 
witnessing exceptional wholesale growth as OEMs stocked 
dealerships ahead of Diwali and allied festivals, followed 
by a natural moderation in December as dealers focused on 
retail sell-through and inventory correction. Looking ahead, 
the industry expects positive momentum to continue well 
into 2026, supported by stable macroeconomic conditions, 
moderated GST improving affordability, and sustained policy 
support. At the same time, close monitoring of geopolitical 
developments will remain critical to ensuring resilience in 
supply chains and export performance.
4. Business & financial overview
4.1 Automotive Technologies
The Automotive Technologies segment, which encompasses 
E‑Mobility, Powertrain and Chassis divisions, continued to 
demonstrate robust growth during CY2025. The segment 
recorded a 24.6% year‑on‑year increase, driven by significant 
business wins in Passenger Vehicle Clutches and Dual Mass 
Flywheels. This segment contributed 33.4% of Schaeffler 
India’s total revenue in CY2025, underscoring its pivotal role 
in the Company’s overall performance and growth trajectory.
Localisation has remained a cornerstone of our strategy, 
enabling us to enhance competitiveness, strengthen supply 
chain resilience, and deliver greater value to customers. By 
leveraging local manufacturing capabilities and engineering 
expertise, we have been able to respond more effectively to 
evolving market demands. During the year, Schaeffler India 
inaugurated its e-axle production line at Talegaon Plant. This 
marked a structural shift from component manufacturing to 
system-level EV drive solutions.
Looking ahead, the Automotive Technologies segment 
is well‑positioned to capitalise on opportunities in 
electrification and advanced mobility solutions. With a 
strong pipeline of innovative products and continued focus 
on localisation, we aim to reinforce our leadership in the 
automotive space.
4.2 Vehicle Lifetime Solutions
The Vehicle Lifetime Solutions segment contributed 12.1% 
of Schaeffler India’s revenue in CY2025. The division saw 
year-on-year growth of 12.2%, supported by continued 
volume wins from new product launches such as wipers, 
and steering & suspension components which remained 
strong contributors, reinforcing customer confidence in our 
aftermarket offerings.
A key highlight during the year was the launch of the 
automotive lube vending machine at the Maneja facility, 
which underscores our commitment to innovation. This 
initiative not only enhances accessibility but also strengthens 
our aftermarket service ecosystem. The segment maintained 
a strategic focus on portfolio expansion and deeper market 
penetration through range extensions, ensuring that 
customers have access to a wider variety of solutions tailored 
to evolving needs.
An important enabler has been our wholly-owned subsidiary 
Koovers, which has provided a significant advantage by 
expanding reach and improving distribution efficiency. 
Koovers’ digital platform has allowed us to connect more 
effectively with workshops and mechanics, thereby 
strengthening customer engagement and ensuring faster 
delivery of parts and solutions.
Looking ahead, Vehicle Lifetime Solutions will continue 
to build on these foundations, leveraging innovation, 
partnerships, and range expansion to drive sustainable 
growth and reinforce Schaeffler’s position in the 
aftermarket space.
4.3 Bearings & Industrial Solutions 
The Bearings & Industrial Solutions segment contributed 
39.2% of Schaeffler India’s revenue in CY2025, reaffirming 
its position as a strong business pillar. The segment 
delivered a 6.4% year-on-year growth, supported by new 
business wins in Deep Groove Ball Bearings and Needle 
Roller Bearings within the two-wheeler segment. 
Further momentum was achieved through business 
nominations for needle bearings and lift mast rollers in the 
off-road segment, strengthening our presence in specialised 
applications and expanding our customer base.
During the year, we inaugurated the Robotic Process 
Automation & Benchmarking Lab at the Maneja facility 
in Vadodara, a milestone that enhances our capability in 
process efficiency, product benchmarking, and innovation. 
This initiative underscores our commitment to leveraging 
technology for operational excellence.
Engagement with channel partners remained a priority, 
highlighted by the Distributor Meet held in Goa, which 
provided a platform to reinforce relationships, share strategic 
updates, and align on future growth opportunities.
Looking ahead, Bearings & Industrial Solutions will continue 
to focus on expanding its product portfolio, deepening 
customer partnerships, deepening localisation, and driving 
innovation to sustain its leadership position in the industrial 
solutions space.

1
Emissions 
management
Risk and 
opportunity
High greenhouse gas (GHG) 
emissions pose several risks 
to the Company, including 
increased operational costs, 
regulatory compliance 
challenges, and reputational 
risks in a market with growing 
sustainability expectations. There 
is a potential risk arising from 
unmet stakeholder expectations 
regarding emissions management.
Operational risks also include 
possible supply chain disruptions 
caused by climate change-related 
events. The Company depends on 
suppliers, primarily in the steel 
sector, to develop lower-carbon 
alternatives through research and 
development, which is critical for 
controlling the carbon footprint 
embedded in its products.
Climate change presents both 
physical risks—such as acute and 
chronic impact on operations and 
the value chain—and transition 
risks, including technological 
changes, evolving market 
demands, and shifting policy 
landscapes.
Schaeffler recognizes the physical 
and transition risks of climate 
change over the short, medium, 
and long term. To address 
these risks, the Company is 
implementing measures to reduce 
greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions 
in the following areas:
Direct emissions from its 
operations (Scope 1 and Scope 2).
Indirect emissions within the 
supply chain (Scope 3).
Additionally, Schaeffler actively 
engages with suppliers to 
identify and adopt sustainable 
alternatives that reduce emissions 
at the source.
Since 2023, Schaeffler has 
adopted Science Based Targets 
initiative (SBTi)-validated climate 
targets aligned with the Paris 
Agreement’s goal to limit global 
warming. Following the merger 
with Vitesco Technologies, these 
targets are currently under review 
to ensure continued alignment 
and revalidation by the SBTi.
Negative financial implications include 
increased operational costs driven by carbon 
pricing mandates and regulatory compliance 
requirements, which enhance transition 
risks. An increase in weather events such as 
storms, floods, and heatwaves could have 
significant direct and indirect impact on our 
supply chain and operations, potentially 
disrupting production and affecting our 
ability to fulfill demand. Additionally, policy 
directions requiring low-carbon manufacturing 
may necessitate capital investments and 
operational changes. Failure to meet 
stakeholder expectations on emissions 
management could lead to reputational 
damage and loss of market share.
On the positive side, investments in emissions 
reduction and sustainable technologies can 
lead to cost savings through improved energy 
efficiency, resource optimisation, and reduced 
carbon footprint. Developing low-carbon 
products and adopting greener supply chain 
practices open new market opportunities and 
strengthen relationships with sustainability-
focused customers. Aligning with global climate 
targets, such as the Science Based Targets 
initiative (SBTi), enhances investor confidence, 
supports access to sustainable financing, and 
positions the Company for long-term resilience.
2
Sustainable 
product 
design
Opportunity 
and risk
Schaeffler India operates in 
the automotive and industrial 
segments where customers 
increasingly demand products 
that meet high standards of 
quality, safety, regulatory 
compliance, and environmental 
performance. Product quality and 
safety are critical to maintaining 
customer trust and long-term OEM 
relationships, while sustainable 
product design—through 
material efficiency, reduced 
environmental footprint, and end-
of-life considerations—supports 
evolving regulatory requirements 
and customer sustainability 
expectations. Continuous R&D 
and technology-led innovation, 
aligned with Schaeffler Group’s 
global R&D agenda, enables the 
development of market-ready, 
safe, and sustainable products, 
strengthening competitiveness 
and supporting long-term growth.
Risks related to product failure, 
safety incidents, or non-compliance 
are mitigated through robust 
quality management systems, a 
strong safety and “zero-defect” 
culture, and group-wide product 
validation and approval processes. 
Sustainability considerations, 
including material compliance, 
reduced use of hazardous 
substances, and end-of-life (EoL) 
integration, are embedded in 
product design and development 
processes. Ongoing investments 
in R&D, innovation governance, 
and technology reviews ensure 
alignment with regulatory, 
customer, and Group sustainability 
requirements.
Positive financial implications include revenue 
growth through stronger OEM relationships, 
market access, and customer preference 
for safe and sustainable products; a pricing 
premium for high-performance and sustainable 
solutions; enhanced competitiveness driven 
by innovation; optimisation of lifecycle costs, 
contributing to sustained business value.
Negative financial implications include 
incremental capital expenditure (capex) and 
operational expenditure (opex) related to R&D 
and design efforts; cost avoidance through the 
reduction of recalls, warranty claims, safety 
incidents, regulatory penalties, and reputational 
damage; and long-term value creation through 
innovation-led competitiveness and lifecycle 
cost optimisation.
3
Safety and 
working 
conditions
Risk
Schaeffler India’s manufacturing 
operations involve significant 
engagement of employees and 
contract workers on the shop floor. 
Any workplace accident, injury, 
or unsafe working condition can 
have serious implications for 
employee well-being, operational 
continuity, regulatory compliance, 
and reputation. While the nature 
of operations limits exposure to 
highly hazardous substances, 
lapses in safety practices or 
unsafe conditions could still result 
in injuries, downtime, and non-
financial impacts that are not easily 
reversible. Therefore, occupational 
health and safety remains a critical 
risk area requiring continuous 
management focus.
The Company has established 
comprehensive occupational 
health and safety management 
systems, supported by both 
proactive and reactive controls. 
These include regular safety 
audits, training and awareness 
programmes, incident reporting 
mechanisms, and defined 
investigation and Root Cause 
Analysis (RCA) processes for any 
incident. Corrective and preventive 
actions are systematically 
implemented to reduce recurrence. 
Continuous monitoring and 
leadership oversight help ensure 
adherence to safety standards 
and improvement in workplace 
conditions.
Losses arising from workplace accidents—
including medical expenses, compensation 
payments, regulatory penalties, litigation 
costs, increased insurance premiums, and 
production downtime—are minimised through 
the implementation of robust safety controls. 
Proactive safety management not only ensures 
operational continuity and protects human 
capital but also helps prevent reputational 
damage and reduces indirect costs linked to 
lost productivity and employee turnover.

Waste 
management
Opportunity
External stakeholders, including 
customers, regulators, and 
communities, increasingly 
expect manufacturers to adopt 
responsible and circular waste 
management practices, including 
reduction of hazardous waste 
and prevention of environmental 
contamination. Given Schaeffler 
India’s manufacturing footprint, 
effective waste management is 
material to meeting stakeholder 
expectations, regulatory 
compliance, and sustainability 
commitments. By focusing on 
waste reduction, reuse, and 
recycling, the Company is able 
to improve resource efficiency 
and support circular economy 
principles across its operations.
Cost optimisation through 
reduced waste disposal expenses 
and improved material efficiency; 
incremental revenue generation 
from the sale of recyclable waste 
streams (e.g., used oil, metal 
scrap); avoidance of regulatory 
penalties and environmental 
remediation costs. Strong waste 
management practices also 
support compliance, operational 
efficiency, and long-term 
sustainability performance.
Positive implications as it helps reduce the 
long-term risk of non-compliance.
5
Data security 
and data 
protection
Risk
Increasing digitalisation of 
enterprise systems, including ERP, 
order management, and customer-
specific engineering data, makes 
data security and privacy critical 
for Schaeffler India. Any data 
breach or cyber incident could 
expose sensitive commercial, 
technical, or personal information, 
disrupt operations, lead to non-
compliance with applicable data 
protection regulations, and impact 
long-term customer trust and OEM 
relationships. Protecting customer 
and proprietary data is therefore 
essential for business continuity 
and reputation.
Schaeffler India addresses data 
security risks through a robust IT 
governance framework, supported 
by Group-wide information 
security policies aligned with 
ISO/IEC 27001 and industry 
standards. Controls include 
access management, regular 
security reviews, cyber threat 
monitoring through a Security 
Operations Centre (SOC), periodic 
audits, and employee awareness 
and training programmes. Incident 
response mechanisms are in 
place to ensure timely detection, 
containment, and remediation of 
cyber incidents.
Avoidance of potential financial losses arising 
from data breaches, including regulatory 
penalties, litigation costs, system downtime, 
loss of customer trust, and reputational 
damage. Ongoing investments in IT security 
infrastructure and governance help protect 
critical data assets, ensure operational 
resilience, and support long-term customer 
relationships.

Does the entity have a specified Committee of the Board/Director responsible for decision-making on sustainability-

The sustainability governance structure at Schaeffler India Limited is formal and well established to oversee ESG and
sustainability issues at all organisational levels. At the top, the Board of Schaeffler India Limited provides overall
governance. The Managing Director & CEO, Harsha Kadam, acts as the sponsor and is supported by the Executive
Leadership Team (ELT).
The Sustainability Head plays a key role in India wide sustainability efforts, participating in a weekly review with the MD & CEO
to ensure alignment. Additionally, a fortnightly huddle connects the Sustainability Head with Plant Sustainability Coordinators 
responsible for the individual plants. This structure is supported by dedicated Functional Representatives focusing on critical 
areas such as sustainable procurement, energy procurement, sustainability reporting, and CSR initiatives, thereby ensuring 
comprehensive oversight and active coordination of sustainability activities across the Company.
1.
The Risk Management Committee (RMC): The RMC formulated a detailed Risk Management Policy covering the
framework for the identification of internal and external risks specifically faced by the Company, particularly
ESG-related risks and measures for risk mitigation. The RMC is responsible for decision-making on sustainability-
related issues. ESG-related risks and opportunities are reviewed by the RMC.
2.	
The Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) Committee: The CSR Committee approves the Annual Action Plan for CSR
Programmes to create a meaningful impact and recommends the same to the Board of Directors for implementation.
The CSR Committee also reviews the status of the CSR projects undertaken towards social cause, contributing to 
sustainability.
3.
Stakeholders’ Relationship Committee (SRC): The SRC Committee is responsible for resolving grievances of the
Shareholders, reviewing measures taken for effective exercise of voting rights, and reviewing initiatives undertaken by
the Company in the interest of the Shareholders.

a.
Does the entity have procedures in place for sustainable sourcing?
Yes
Sustainability is integral to Schaeffler’s core values, focusing on identifying, managing, and optimising ecological,
social, and economic impacts throughout our supplier network. Recognising that raw materials for modern technologies
often come from geopolitically sensitive areas, and given the challenges posed by climate change and resource scarcity,
we actively strengthen partnerships with our suppliers to promote and embed sustainable practices collaboratively.
Our sustainable sourcing framework includes the following key elements:
Business Partner Code of Conduct
All Schaeffler India suppliers are required to acknowledge Business Partner Code of Conduct, which explicitly
addresses responsible sourcing, including conflict minerals and critical raw materials.
Sustainability Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ)
As per group guidelines, suppliers undergo a phased Sustainability Self-Assessment Questionnaire covering critical
areas such as Company Management, Human Rights and Working Conditions, Health and Safety, Business Ethics,
Environmental Stewardship, Responsible Supply Chain Management, and Responsible Sourcing of Raw Materials.
Incorporation of Sustainability in Sourcing Approval
Sustainability criteria form a part of the sourcing approval process to ensure alignment with our standards.
Sustainability Target Agreement (STA)
We enter into mutual agreement named "Sustainability Target Agreement" with selected production material suppliers
to drive continuous improvement in sustainability performance. These targets cover Greenhouse Gas Emissions,
Renewable Energy adoption, Waste Management, Human Rights Due Diligence, Returnable Packaging, and other
relevant aspects, following group guidelines.
Conflict Minerals Reporting
Schaeffler adheres strictly to the group’s Conflict Minerals Reporting Procedure to maintain an ethical supply chain
and comply with responsible sourcing requirements.
This structured approach helps us in mitigating supply chain risks and fosters responsible business practices
throughout our sourcing ecosystem.

Describe the processes in place to safely reclaim your products for reuse, recycling and disposal at the end of their life.
Our Bearing Refurbishing Centre is a facility dedicated to the refurbishment and maintenance of bearings, mainly aimed at
extending the life of bearings, reducing operational costs, and supporting sustainability by minimising waste and resource
consumption. Refurbishment of bearings plays an important role in extending the lifecycle of product solutions and
reducing CO2 emissions, thereby saving significant amounts of resources (sustainability focus).
• By refurbishing bearings, the centre promotes a circular economy approach.
• Reduces waste and conserves materials by extending the usable life of existing bearings.
• Supports Schaeffler’s overall sustainability goals by minimising environmental impact.
Additionally, all products comply with European regulations such as ELV, RoHS, and REACH, supporting the safe disposal 
of products at the end of their life..
(a)	Plastics 
(including packaging)
Plastic waste generated from our manufacturing and warehousing locations is responsibly managed by recycling 
it through an authorised recycler, ensuring compliance with environmental regulations and standards.
(b)	E-waste
E-waste generated from all Company locations is safely managed by either recycling it through an authorised 
recycler or sending it back to the original manufacturer.
(c) Hazardous waste
Waste generated from manufacturing locations is sent to authorised recyclers or for co-processing, enabling 
Schaeffler India to achieve Zero Waste to Landfill status across all plant locations.
(d)	Other waste.
Metal scraps generated from the manufacturing process are recycled responsibly by either returning them to 
suppliers or sending them to authorised recyclers.

a.
Whether an occupational health and safety management system has been implemented by the entity? (Yes/No). If
yes, the coverage of such a system?
Yes.
Safety is a fundamental value that takes precedence over all business objectives at Schaeffler. Each of our plants is
equipped with Occupational Health Centre (OHC) facilities staffed by doctors, nurses, and ambulances operating 24/7
to ensure prompt medical care. Our health and safety management systems are implemented in accordance with the
international standard ISO 45001 (Occupational Health and Safety Management System), reflecting our commitment
to maintaining a safe and healthy work environment across all the locations of Schaeffler India Ltd.
EnEHS Policy – Group      ISO 45001
b.
What are the processes used to identify work-related hazards and assess risks on a routine and non-routine basis by
the entity?
Schaeffler India prioritises safety as a core responsibility, committed to fostering a strong safety culture across all
organisational levels. The Company continuously evaluates safety practices against industry standards to ensure a
secure workplace for employees, business partners, and contractors. A comprehensive risk management system is
in place involving risk identification, assessment, and mitigation through multi-level processes and regular audits,
supported by awareness programmes and emergency preparedness. Safety is integral to business operations, with
emphasis on instilling a culture of safety throughout the organisation.
Hazard Identification and Assessment (HIRA)
• Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA) is conducted regularly at all locations
• Three-stage process involving local cross-functional teams and third-party engagement
Systems and Processes to Identify Risks
• Regular workplace inspections using TPM checklists to spot hazards and unsafe practices
• EHS walkthroughs involving cross-functional teams and top management for comprehensive safety reviews
• Group internal safety audits and external audits aligned with ISO 45001 standards
• Near-miss reporting system actively encourages employees on the shop floor to report potential incidents
• Detailed risk assessments for every machine within the plant
• Well-prepared location-specific evacuation plans with mapped fire extinguisher locations prominently displayed
Employee Awareness
• Continuous safety awareness initiatives are conducted to educate and engage employees on occupational safety.

Whether you have processes for workers to report the work-related hazards and to remove themselves from such risks (Y/N)
Yes.
Schaeffler India actively encourages employees and workers to report health and safety violations, including work
hazards, near misses, and unsafe acts, through multiple channels.
These include:
• Daily shop floor meetings: Provide an opportunity for workers to report incidents or potential hazards regularly.
• Plant safety officers: Each site has designated safety officers who receive reports, investigate incidents, and
develop action plans when required.
• Group-level reporting: A centralised incident reporting system enables any employee across locations to report
issues, which are managed in coordination with EHS regional and central functions.
This multi-tiered approach ensures timely incident detection, thorough investigation, and effective resolution to
prevent recurrence.

programmes such as yoga, periodic health assessments, and workplace inspections. Additionally, the Company conducts

Schaeffler India’s social responsibility is anchored in HOPE, our flagship CSR framework that drives integrated and long-
term community impact across geographies. Our efforts span four core pillars:
Healthcare
We deliver last-mile primary healthcare through mobile health units, with a strong focus on preventive and curative 
healthcare. Our initiatives strengthen maternal and child health, reduce anaemia, and support communities in accessing 
government health schemes—ensuring improved health outcomes for underserved populations.
Occupational skilling
Our skilling ecosystem comprises industry-aligned technical and vocational training centres and dedicated women 
skill development programmes. These initiatives enhance employability, build entrepreneurial capabilities, and create 
sustainable livelihood opportunities for underprivileged youth and women.
Preservation of environment
Through natural resource management and climate-resilient agriculture initiatives, Schaeffler India promotes watershed 
development, soil and water conservation, and improved agricultural practices. We further empower rural communities 
by strengthening farmer collectives and village development committees to ensure long-term environmental sustainability.
Empowerment of society
We advance education and community development through support for STEM learning, pre-vocational skilling (IBT), and 
scholarship programs. In addition, we foster social innovation by partnering with IIMA Ventures for mentorship support. 
Together, these initiatives contribute to building inclusive, resilient, and future-ready communities.

Mechanisms to prevent adverse consequences to the complainant in discrimination and harassment cases
The Schaeffler India Limited has established formal mechanisms to ensure protection of complainants and prevent
retaliation in cases of discrimination or harassment.
-
Anonymous reporting: Complaints can be reported through the Schaeffler Whistle-Blower platform (SpeakUp system),
which allows anonymous reporting and is accessible only to the Compliance function.
	-
Confidentiality: Complaints are handled with strict confidentiality to protect the identity of complainants and witnesses.
-
Anti-retaliation: The Company follows a zero-tolerance policy against retaliation. Any adverse action against
complainants or witnesses is subject to disciplinary action.
-
Fair investigation: Complaints are investigated in a timely, impartial, and unbiased manner by trained internal teams or
external experts, as applicable.
	-
Support mechanisms: Appropriate support measures are provided to complainants during and after the investigation process.
-
Multiple reporting channels: Complaints may also be reported through HR, designated Ethics or Compliance Officers,
or other internal grievance redressal mechanisms. These mechanisms are designed to ensure a safe, secure, and
non-retaliatory environment for individuals raising concerns.

10.	 Briefly describe the waste management practices adopted in your establishments. Describe the strategy adopted by your 
Company to reduce usage of hazardous and toxic chemicals in your products and processes and the practices adopted to 
manage such waste.
We align our waste and resource management approach with India’s Hazardous Waste Management Rules and global 
circular economy principles, prioritising waste prevention, material efficiency, and value recovery across operations. Our 
strategy focuses on minimising resource extraction, maximising material circularity, and eliminating landfill dependency.
•	 Schaeffler India achieved 97% waste recycling and recovery and achieved Zero Waste to Landfill status as of December 31, 2025.
•	 This has significantly reduced environmental burden by preventing land, soil, and groundwater contamination, 
minimising methane emissions from landfill disposal, and supporting Scope 3 emission reduction efforts.
•	 We are advancing waste-to-value initiatives by integrating circular design and operational excellence. A notable example 
includes converting foundry waste such as casting moulding sand—traditionally associated with ~50% wastage—into 
construction bricks, which were utilised in our greenfield projects, demonstrating closed-loop material integration.
•	 Hazardous waste streams, including ETP sludge and grinding sludge, are responsibly managed through authorised 
co-processing in cement kilns, reducing landfill reliance and enabling energy and material recovery. During the 
reporting period, 854.7 tonnes of hazardous waste was diverted for co-processing, ensuring environmentally sound 
treatment aligned with circular economy principles.
•	 We maintain strict compliance with global chemical management frameworks including REACH and RoHS, supported by 
a robust Declarable Substances Register, along with ongoing monitoring, verification, and supplier engagement.
•	 Further, we enable internal water circularity ensuring complete reuse of treated wastewater for process and 
utility applications.
•	 Returnable and reusable packaging solutions are deployed across the value chain to enhance resource efficiency, 
reduce waste intensity, and lower lifecycle environmental impacts.

focused on hazard prevention, ensuring uninterrupted customer supply, and effective crisis response. We have internal

defines escalation stages for incidents, integrates IT disaster recovery, and employs a risk management system with
structured risk reporting and mitigation.

Deliver a clear regulatory framework for business continuity, with emphasis on:
• Contingency management to prevent hazards and maintain customer supply.
• Crisis management to manage and respond to serious incidents.

• Disruption
• Emergency
• Emergency with crisis potential
• Local/regional crisis
• Mandatory reporting of any situation, even if outside these categories, to maintain vigilance.

• Facilitates coordination across departments to manage emergencies effectively.
4.

• Comprehensive Information Technology Disaster Recovery Plan complements the Business Continuity Plan.

production, distribution, and support functions.

• Regulates technical, organisational, environmental, and safety measures to protect personnel and equipment.

unforeseen risks like supply chain disruptions etc.

Opinion Statement 
We have conducted a reasonable assurance engagement on the sustainability information described in the 
“Scope” above (BRSR for CY 2025 covering core KPIs mentioned in Annexure-I: format of BRSR core, 
provided by SEBI, covering disclosures on Green-house gas (GHG) footprint, Water footprint, Energy 
footprint, Embracing Circularity, Enhancing Employee Wellbeing and Safety, Enabling Gender Diversity in 
Business, Enabling Inclusive Development, Fairness in Engaging with Customers and Suppliers, Open-ness 
of business).   
In our opinion, the accompanying sustainability information is fairly presented, in all material aspects, in 
accordance with the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR Core KPI’s) for the reporting 
period 1st January 2025 to 31st December 2025. 
Methodology 
Our assurance engagements were carried out in accordance with ISAE3000 (Revised) assurance standard 
following the principles of Integrity, Objectivity, Professional competence and due care, Confidentiality, and 
Professional behaviour. ISO 14064-3:2019 assurance standard is used for information related to GHG 
statement.  Our work was designed to gather evidence on which to base our opinion conclusions. 
We undertook the following activities: 
•
Assessment of the organization’s reporting and management processes concerning this reporting against
the principles of relevance, completeness, reliability, neutrality, understandability.
•
Data verification on reasonable level sampling including asking for internal controls and implementation
of internal controls, SOPs for data gathering and reporting mechanism.
•
Interviews with staffs involved in sustainability management, BRSR report preparation and ESG data
management and calculation of final numbers.
•
Document review of relevant systems, policies, and procedures wherever available.
•
Review of supporting evidence for claims made in the reports.
•
Traceability of information from the origin and testing at site for measurement procedures
•
Review of data pertaining to the sampled units of TSIL, to confirm the data collection processes, record
management practices, and check BRSR Core KPI’s physically and through virtual mode. 
Responsibility 
Schaeffler India Limited (SIL) is responsible for the preparation and fair presentation of the sustainability 
information in accordance with the agreed criteria. BSI is responsible for providing an independent assurance 
opinion statement to stakeholders giving our professional opinion based on the scope and methodology 
described.
